My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across the three horizons, anchored to what was likely a recent observed price or index level near 77–78. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 77.8 is essentially a near-random-walk projection, weighted heavily by momentum and mean-reversion tendencies over very short periods. The incremental increases are small because I'm not assuming any strong directional catalyst, just a baseline drift in a relatively stable environment.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which is the expected behavior under standard diffusion-style uncertainty. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 6.4 units, which corresponds to typical daily volatility scaled appropriately. By one week, the interval nearly doubles to about 14.4 units, reflecting that weekly price variance scales roughly with the square root of time. At one month, the interval balloons to nearly 30 units, capturing the compounding uncertainty over roughly 20 trading days. The asymmetry or near-symmetry in the intervals at each horizon suggests I was not heavily weighting skewed tail risks in either direction, though the absolute width at one month is wide enough to capture a meaningful range of macro-driven scenarios.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these intervals include sudden macroeconomic shocks such as an unexpected central bank policy decision, a geopolitical escalation, or a significant earnings surprise if this is an individual equity. A sharp risk-off episode driven by credit stress or liquidity withdrawal could push prices well below the lower bounds, particularly at the one-week and one-month horizons. On the upside, a strong positive catalyst — a merger announcement, a better-than-expected inflation reading, or a policy pivot — could push the asset above 94 at the one-month horizon or beyond. Structural breaks in volatility regimes, such as a sudden spike in the VIX or a correlation breakdown among assets, represent the most dangerous tail scenarios because they invalidate the diffusion assumptions underlying my interval construction entirely.
